analysis.disclaimer: The event analysis is assisted by an AI model and can be wrong, in both directions (an attack taken for normal use, or the reverse). Its conclusions are suggestions only: loosening (exclusions, allowing) always needs a person's approval; only tightening (a new confident block) may apply on its own, and only when every check passed. Look at the evidence yourself before you approve.
analysis.err.bad_json: Cause: the model's answer was not the JSON asked for. Use a model that follows JSON output, or check that the server supports JSON schemas.
analysis.err.bad_reply: Cause: the model answered JSON, but not what was asked (a candidate missing, a verdict out of range). The batch is not used; the next run asks again.
analysis.err.bad_response: Cause: the LLM server's answer was not a chat completion. Check that the URL points to an OpenAI-compatible API; the log below shows the start of the answer.
analysis.err.http_500: Cause: an internal error on the LLM server (500). See what the server answered in the log below and check the LLM server's own log.
analysis.err.http_502: Cause: the LLM server or a gateway in front of it answered 502: it could not answer at that moment (a model loading, busy, or the server just restarted). It was tried again after a wait; the next scheduled run usually works. If it keeps failing, check the LLM server.
analysis.err.http_503: Cause: the LLM server is unavailable for the moment (503). It was tried again after a wait; if it keeps failing, check the LLM server.
analysis.err.http_504: Cause: the gateway in front of the LLM server gave up waiting (504). A smaller or faster model, fewer candidates per batch, or a longer gateway timeout helps.
analysis.err.internal_error: Cause: an internal error in this program. Report the log below together with the event analysis service's system log (journalctl).
analysis.err.model_not_found: Cause: the model chosen in Settings is not on the LLM server. Test the connection again and pick a model.
analysis.err.not_configured: Cause: the LLM server URL is not set.
analysis.err.not_found: Cause: the LLM server does not know this address (404). Check that the URL in Settings ends in /v1.
analysis.err.other: See the error log below for the cause.
analysis.err.output_truncated: Cause: the model's answer went past the output limit and was cut short (often a reasoning model thinking at length). The limit was raised and the question asked again up to the maximum, and it was still not enough; use a model that thinks less, or turn thinking off for JSON answers on the LLM server.
analysis.err.response_too_large: Cause: the LLM server's answer was too large and was not processed.
analysis.err.timeout: Cause: the LLM server did not answer within the timeout. Raise the timeout in Settings, use a faster model, or send fewer candidates per batch.
analysis.err.token_limit: Cause: the first-tier LLM token limit was reached; the remaining candidates were not judged this time. The limit is in Settings → first-tier LLM.
analysis.err.unauthorized: Cause: the LLM server refused the API key (401/403). Enter the API key again in Settings.
analysis.err.unreachable: Cause: the LLM server could not be reached (connection refused, name not found or no route). Check the URL in Settings, that the server runs, and that this host can reach it.

bundle.evidence_note: Each operation is judged on its own; the change passes only when every one passes.
bundle.ops_note: All of them are checked, approved and applied together: one version, one nginx reload, and one rollback undoes them all.
cfgchg.diff_none: Not shown: a version of this file was not stored (not text, larger than 512 KB, or changed before this version kept file contents).
cfgchg.diff_same: No difference in the stored text (only masked values or whitespace changed).
cfgchg.diffs_before: What changed in the files is not shown: this change was recorded before file contents were kept (0.4.30).
cfgchg.diffs_hint: The stored text of each file before and after. Values after words such as password, token or key, and long random-looking strings, are masked before they are stored.
cfgchg.intro: Every few minutes every nginx, ModSecurity and CRS file, the nginx binary and the ModSecurity module are fingerprinted (SHA-256). Each change is recorded and attributed: an applied version, or a change from outside (manual edit, package upgrade…).
cfgchg.title: Configuration changes
cfgchg.who_hint: From the host's authentication log, between the previous check and this one. A lead, not proof: an open session is not necessarily the one that changed the file, and a local program (a package update, a scheduled job) leaves no login.
cfgchg.who_live: Recorded before the logins were kept: looked up now in the host's authentication log (older logins may have been rotated away).
cfgchg.who_none: No login in the host's authentication log in that time: a local program, or a log that is not readable.

compliance.ctl.account_management.desc: Accounts can have an end date and are disabled after it; accounts without a sign-in for the configured number of days are disabled automatically (never the last active administrator); the account review lists every account and token for the periodic review.
compliance.ctl.account_management.title: Account management
compliance.ctl.audit_logging.desc: Every action is recorded with time, actor, actor type, source address, action, result and details, and sent as one JSON line to syslog.
compliance.ctl.audit_logging.title: Audit logging
compliance.ctl.auth_feedback.desc: Passwords and codes are masked while typed; an unknown user and a wrong password get the same answer and the same response time.
compliance.ctl.auth_feedback.title: Authenticator feedback
compliance.ctl.authentication.desc: Passwords are stored as scrypt hashes; minimum length, character classes, history and minimum / maximum age are enforced; accounts are locked after repeated failures; a temporary password must be changed at the first sign-in.
compliance.ctl.authentication.title: Password authentication
compliance.ctl.backup.desc: A daily database backup is made with an integrity check and a SHA-256 file and kept for the configured days; copying the backups off the host is an organisational measure.
compliance.ctl.backup.title: Backup
compliance.ctl.change_management.desc: Rule changes go through static checks, evidence, a sandbox and an approval; a root program applies them with nginx -t, reload, health check and automatic restore; every version can be rolled back.
compliance.ctl.change_management.title: Change management
Every nginx, ModSecurity and CRS file, the nginx binary and the ModSecurity module are fingerprinted; every change is recorded and attributed, and manual edits of the managed rule files are detected.
compliance.ctl.data_at_rest.desc: The database is readable only by the service user (file 0600, directory 0700) and holds masked values only; it is not encrypted by the program, so use disk encryption where it is required.
compliance.ctl.data_at_rest.title: Stored data
compliance.ctl.data_masking.desc: Values of sensitive parameters (passwords, tokens, one-time codes…) are masked before anything is stored; there is no way to see the original.
compliance.ctl.data_masking.title: Masking of sensitive data
compliance.ctl.evidence_export.desc: The audit log can be exported with every hash and a summary hash and verified offline; event exports carry a SHA-256.
compliance.ctl.evidence_export.title: Evidence export
compliance.ctl.least_privilege.desc: Four roles (viewer, operator, approver, administrator). API tokens are limited to scopes and source networks and can never approve changes, manage tokens or change settings.
compliance.ctl.least_privilege.title: Least privilege
compliance.ctl.log_capacity.desc: Free disk space is checked against a minimum; events, statistics and the audit log have configured retention periods.
compliance.ctl.log_capacity.title: Log storage capacity
compliance.ctl.log_failure_response.desc: Integrity failures, failed backups and account lockouts are written as critical events (syslog priority 2) so the SIEM can alert; syslog delivery errors are counted on the system check.
compliance.ctl.log_protection.desc: Records are hash-chained and the table refuses changes and deletions; every few minutes the newest hash is anchored in an append-only file and in syslog, so a rewritten chain is detected.
compliance.ctl.log_protection.title: Protection of the audit log
compliance.ctl.monitoring.desc: The web application firewall events themselves: blocked and logged requests by site, attack type, source and rule, plus every configuration change.
compliance.ctl.monitoring.title: Monitoring
compliance.ctl.multi_factor.desc: Time-based one-time codes (TOTP) are required for the configured roles (by default approver and administrator), with protection against reusing a code.
compliance.ctl.multi_factor.title: Two-factor authentication
compliance.ctl.retention.desc: Events and statistics are deleted after the configured days; the audit log is kept forever by default, and a configured purge keeps the remaining chain verifiable.
compliance.ctl.retention.title: Retention
compliance.ctl.secure_development.desc: The backend uses the Python standard library only; the interface has a strict content security policy and shows request data as text only; automated tests and a release check (privacy scan, tests) run before every release.
compliance.ctl.secure_development.title: Secure development
compliance.ctl.segregation_of_duties.des: Whoever proposes a change cannot approve it. Single-admin mode (recorded in the audit log) allows it, with a fresh one-time code and a written reason for any loosening.
compliance.ctl.session_timeout.desc: Idle sessions are signed out automatically, every session has a maximum lifetime, and the number of sessions per user is limited.
compliance.ctl.session_timeout.title: Session timeout
compliance.ctl.siem_forwarding.desc: Audit records and anchors are written to the local syslog as JSON; forwarding them to the SIEM and the alert rules are set up in the syslog daemon and the SIEM.
compliance.ctl.siem_forwarding.title: Forwarding to the SIEM
compliance.ctl.software_integrity.desc: Each release ships a manifest with the SHA-256 of every file, signed with the release key (RSA-3072). The installer verifies it and pins the key; the service and the root apply program check the installed files again, and the apply program refuses to run modified code.
compliance.ctl.software_integrity.title: Software integrity

guide.adopt.approve_d: Adoption is a change of its own and only an administrator can approve it.
guide.adopt.detect_d: The local Include files of the main ModSecurity file: the last one before the CRS rules and the first one after them.
guide.adopt.drift_fix: To fix it: if the edit was not wanted, either undo it on the server, or (approver) restore the files of the current version below — that overwrites the edit and is recorded in the audit trail. If the edit was wanted, restore first and then propose the same rule here as a change.
guide.adopt.drift_what: After every apply the hashes of the managed files are recorded. When a file on disk no longer matches the last applied version, someone edited it outside this system. Every change and restore is then refused (and recorded at priority crit), so the edit is never overwritten silently; the root apply program checks the same hashes again right before it writes.
guide.adopt.equiv_d: The sandbox sends recent distinct requests from the event history plus the regression samples through the current and the new configuration: every status code and matched rule must be identical.
guide.adopt.import_d: Every rule and comment block is copied unchanged, in file order.
guide.adopt.managed_d: From then on only this tool writes these files, and every change goes through checks and approval.
guide.adopt.switch_d: The apply program writes the two managed files, points the Include lines of the main ModSecurity file at them, then runs nginx -t, reload and the health checks.
guide.adopt.title: Adoption: from hand-made files to managed files
guide.analysis.approve_d: An approver approves or rejects it in Changes. A rejected path is not proposed again for 30 days.
guide.analysis.candidates_d: Events grouped by the path a rule sees (decoded, lowercase, no query). Kept with enough events and sources; left out when an existing rule or an open change covers the path, or a proposal for it was turned down in the last 30 days.
guide.analysis.checks_d: The usual checks: the rule itself, evidence from the access logs (no external 2xx/3xx, no internal requests) and the sandbox.
guide.analysis.events_d: WAF events of the last hours: external requests no confident rule stopped yet (attack probes), and requests the anomaly score blocked (false positives).
guide.analysis.llm_d: Sent to the configured LLM server in batches (at most 15 each), the answer constrained by a JSON schema: a verdict per path (attack probe, legitimate, unsure; for blocked requests false positive, attack, unsure), a confidence and a reason, plus a regular expression for attack probes. The request data is always marked untrusted.
guide.analysis.note: The analysis never approves and never writes rules itself. Loosening (exclusions for false positives) and blocks that include internal sources always wait for a person; only external confident blocks apply by themselves, when you turn on "Apply the event analysis' confident blocks automatically too" and the evidence and sandbox checks pass.
guide.analysis.propose_d: Only a few per run: external confident blocks and the narrowest exclusions, proposed as ordinary changes by "analyst"; what needs following up becomes an alert and is notified.
guide.analysis.title: How the analysis works
guide.analysis.validate_d: The program decides, not the model: only attack probes with enough confidence; the regex must start with ^, match the path, and not match common paths, paths judged legitimate or regression samples.
guide.apply.drift_d: The managed files must still be the ones the change was prepared against; otherwise it refuses.
guide.apply.health_after_d: The same URLs again: every status code must be unchanged.
guide.apply.health_before_d: Requests every health check URL through this nginx and notes the status codes.
guide.apply.note: Any failure from the write on puts the snapshot back, runs nginx -t and reloads again: the change shows “apply failed (restored)”. A failure before the snapshot (bad request, manual edit) changes nothing.
guide.apply.reload_d: Reloads nginx, confirms that new worker processes started, then waits for the old ones to finish.
guide.apply.request_d: Checksums, allowed directives and the rule ID range are checked again; nginx must be running its installed binary.
guide.apply.snapshot_d: Copies the current files aside so they can be put back.
guide.apply.title: Inside the apply program
guide.apply.write_d: Writes the new managed files (adoption: also points the main ModSecurity file at them).
guide.arch.hint: Click a box (or focus it and press Enter) to read what it does.
guide.arch.service: service user jtwaf, listens on 127.0.0.1 only
guide.arch.title: Architecture
guide.audit.alert_d: A failure writes integrity.audit_chain_failed at syslog priority crit, repeated every 12 hours while it lasts, and a _recovered record once it is fixed.
guide.audit.anchor_d: Every few minutes (default 5, [integrity] anchor_minutes) the newest record number and hash are appended to the anchor file (append-only, chattr +a) and sent to syslog for the SIEM. Each record also goes to syslog with its hash.
guide.audit.chain_d: Each record stores sha256(previous record's hash + this record). Changing, inserting or removing a record breaks the chain from that point on.
guide.audit.note: Export gives every record with its hashes, so the file can be checked offline with the audit-verify command shown after the export.
guide.audit.row_d: Sign-ins, changes, approvals, settings and system tasks each write one record (time, who, from where, what, result). The table only accepts new records: database triggers refuse changes and deletions.
guide.audit.title: How the audit trail is protected
guide.audit.verify_d: New records are checked at every anchor run, the whole chain once a day, and on demand with "Verify chain" or "Run checks now".
guide.cfgchg.cause_d: Applied version: only managed files changed, they match the last applied version and a version was applied around that time. Anything else: outside.
guide.cfgchg.compare_d: If the overall fingerprint differs from the last snapshot, the added, removed and changed files are listed. The first snapshot is the baseline.
guide.cfgchg.note: Look at every outside change: who made it and why.
guide.cfgchg.record_d: A new snapshot is saved and a config.changed audit record is written (result "outside" for outside changes).
guide.cfgchg.scan_d: Every few minutes (default 5, [integrity] config_check_minutes) the SHA-256 of every nginx, ModSecurity, CRS and managed file and of the nginx program is taken.
guide.cfgchg.title: How configuration changes are found
guide.cfgchg.warn_d: An outside change makes System check show a warning for 7 days.
guide.change.apply_d: The root apply program saves the current files, writes the new ones, runs nginx -t and reloads.
guide.change.approve_d: Loosening always needs a person, by default not the proposer. Tightening is applied automatically only if an admin turned that on, under strict conditions.
guide.change.checks_d: Static checks (regex sanity, too broad, ReDoS shape, rule-id ranges) and what the change would have done to past traffic.
guide.change.note: Every step is in the audit trail, and every apply keeps a version you can roll back to.
guide.change.propose_d: Pick a template (exclusion, confident block, redaction, plugin toggle, expert rule) and the narrowest scope.
guide.change.sandbox_d: A temporary nginx on 127.0.0.1 runs the test requests and the regression samples.
guide.change.title: From proposal to production
guide.change.verify_d: It confirms the reload took effect and the health-check URLs answer as before; any failure restores the previous files.
guide.compliance.fix_d: Edit {path}, restart the service, then Refresh. "Download JSON" keeps the result as evidence.
guide.compliance.level_d_set: Set to {level} by [compliance] level in config.toml. Higher levels add stricter requirements.
guide.compliance.level_d_unset: Not set ([compliance] level in config.toml): controls are judged on the basic checks only. medium and high add stricter requirements, such as password rules, dormant accounts and, at high, two-factor authentication for every role.
guide.compliance.live_d: Each control is computed now from the running configuration and the latest integrity checks, not from a questionnaire.
guide.compliance.needs_d: Under a gap or a partial control, the list names the setting or step that would close it, for example auth.password_history>=3.
guide.compliance.note: Each control cites ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A, the Taiwan protection baseline and OWASP Top 10:2025. Only what the code actually does is claimed.
guide.compliance.status_d: Met: done by the software. Partial: done in part. Gap: missing at this level. Organisational measure: needs a process outside the software (for example SIEM review or patching).
guide.compliance.title: How to read this page
guide.crs.compare_d: The total is compared with the inbound threshold ({n}).
guide.crs.pl_d: Rules up to this level count toward blocking; rules up to a higher detection level only add to the log. Higher levels catch more, and cause more false positives.
guide.crs.points_d: By severity: critical 5, error 4, warning 3, notice 2 (CRS defaults).
guide.crs.result_d: At or over the threshold: 403 if the engine is on for that request; in detection-only mode it is only logged.
guide.crs.title: How OWASP CRS scores a request
guide.cstate.apply_failed: Applying failed; the previous files were restored automatically.
guide.cstate.applying: The apply program is writing the files and reloading nginx.
guide.cstate.approved: Approved; waiting for its turn at the apply program.
guide.cstate.failed: A check did not pass. Run the checks again or propose a corrected change.
guide.cstate.pending_approval: Every check passed; waiting for an approver.
guide.cstate.rejected: An approver rejected it, with a note.
guide.cstate.rolled_back: Was in production; an earlier version was restored later.
guide.detail.internal: Stopped by an internal error; the previous files were restored.
guide.detail.not_this_kind: Not a step for this kind of change
guide.detail.overridden: Did not pass; overridden with a justification
guide.detail.rolled_back: Replaced later by restoring an earlier version
guide.detail.title: Where this change stands
guide.ev.audit_d: ModSecurity writes the request and every rule it matched to its JSON audit log.
guide.ev.collect_d: The collector picks up new lines every few seconds, masks passwords and tokens, marks the source internal or external with the internal address list from the settings, and stores the result.
guide.ev.decide_d: An external source is blocked with 403 when it hits a confident-block rule, or when its score reaches the CRS inbound threshold (if blocking over the threshold is switched on). Internal addresses and everything else are only logged.
guide.ev.list_d: One row per request. Open a row to see the rules it matched, then decide whether a change is needed.
guide.ev.note: "Blocked" means the engine was on for that request and the answer was 403 (or 400 for a malformed request body). "Decided by" tells which rule made the call: a confident rule, the CRS score, the fallback rule or another rule.
guide.ev.request_d: A browser, app or scanner sends a request to one of the sites behind nginx.
guide.ev.rules_d: Every CRS rule that matches adds points to the request's anomaly score. The site's own rules (exclusions, confident blocks) run in the same pass.
guide.ev.title: How a request becomes an event here
guide.evd.decide_d: Legitimate request blocked: create an exclusion. Attack that got through: create a similar block. Expected result: nothing to do.
guide.evd.title: Where this event stands
guide.first.check_d: System check shows the service, integrity, time sync and backups at a glance (admin).
guide.first.events_d: Filter by site, outcome, rule or source; open one to see the request and every rule it hit.
guide.first.lookup_d: Everything one source did, to tell a false positive from an attack.
guide.first.overview_d: Blocked and logged traffic over time; the top sites, attack types, sources and rules.
guide.first.propose_d: Exclude a false positive or block an attack (operator and above); it then goes through checks, the sandbox and approval.
guide.first.signin_d: Change the temporary password; approvers and admins set up TOTP.
guide.first.title: First sign-in
guide.intro: What each part does, the first things to look at, how a rule change travels from proposal to production, and what each role may do.
guide.ip.attack: Real attack? Propose a confident block
guide.ip.attack_d: From an event, "Create similar block" drafts a rule for the same path. It only blocks external sources.
guide.ip.events_d: Look at the paths, the status codes and whether the requests were blocked.
guide.ip.fp_d: Open one of its events and use "Create exclusion for this": the draft is limited to that site and path, and to the rules and fields it matched.
guide.ip.look_d: See how many events it caused in 7 and 30 days, on which sites, and which rules it hit.
guide.ip.note: Nothing changes on the site until a change passes the checks and the sandbox test and is approved by a person. Confident-block rules never block internal addresses.
guide.ip.rules_d: Open a rule to read what it looks for and how often it fires for everyone else.
guide.ip.title: How to investigate a source address
guide.node.access.desc: nginx writes one line per request. Only numbers per site and hour are added up from them (requests, status codes, bytes sent, external share); no address or URL is kept. The Traffic page and the periodic WAF review use them.
guide.node.access.name: Access logs
guide.node.analyst.desc: Groups recent events into candidates on a schedule and asks the configured LLM server in batches; the program validates the answer, proposes narrow blocks or exclusions as ordinary changes and opens alerts for what needs following up. It never approves or writes rules; loosening always waits for a person.
guide.node.analyst.name: Event analysis
guide.node.apply.desc: The only part that runs as root, started by systemd when an approved change is queued. It validates the request again, saves the current files, checks the health-check URLs, writes the new files, runs nginx -t, reloads, confirms the reload took effect and checks the URLs again. Any failure restores the previous files. It refuses to run when its own files do not match the signed release.
guide.node.apply.name: Apply program
guide.node.auditlog.desc: ModSecurity writes one JSON record for each request that matched rules: the request, every rule it hit, the score and whether it was blocked.
guide.node.auditlog.name: Audit log
guide.node.channels.desc: E-mail, Telegram, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Discord, Zulip, Nextcloud Talk and a generic webhook (HMAC signature). Values from requests never become markup, links or mentions.
guide.node.channels.name: Channels
guide.node.clients.desc: Browsers, apps and bots on the internet and on the internal network. Every request reaches nginx first.
guide.node.clients.name: Visitors
guide.node.collector.desc: Follows the audit log, turns every record into an event and stores it with hourly statistics. It also counts the requests in the nginx access logs per site and hour (numbers only).
guide.node.collector.name: Collector
guide.node.database.desc: SQLite: events, statistics, changes, versions, accounts and the hash-chained audit trail. File mode 0600, owned by the service user; sensitive request values are masked before they are stored.
guide.node.database.name: Database
guide.node.intel.desc: The second LLM layer. Every few hours (3 by default) it looks up public vulnerability reports for the confirmed list of web applications: a cloud model searches by itself, an on-premises one through an MCP web search. Only product names and versions leave; never requests, addresses or site names. For a vulnerability that affects this site it drafts a precaution rule that looks only at the URL or headers, which goes through the usual checks and sandbox; one exploited in the wild that is not patched here comes first, with an urgent notification.
guide.node.intel.name: Threat intel
guide.node.iprep.desc: Its own restricted service: public IP lists (Spamhaus DROP, FireHOL, Emerging Threats, Feodo, CINS, blocklist.de and others) downloaded once a day and matched on this host; when someone looks up an outside address, Shodan InternetDB and the organisation's MISP are asked online. Only that outside address is sent; the web service itself never connects out. The results go to the database and show on the IP lookup page and with the events.
guide.node.iprep.name: IP reputation
guide.node.ipsources.desc: Public IP denylists (downloaded once a day, replaced as a whole after checking), Shodan InternetDB (one address asked online) and the organisation's own MISP (a read-only key, a pinned certificate fingerprint if wanted). Only the IP reputation service connects to them.
guide.node.ipsources.name: Reputation sources
guide.node.llm.desc: The OpenAI-compatible LLM server of the event analysis (llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama...), set in Settings. Request data goes only here, so keep it on your own premises. The data sent to it is always marked untrusted; the answer is constrained by a JSON schema.
guide.node.llm.name: LLM, first layer
guide.node.llm2.desc: The model of the threat intel: OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic. An on-premises model works with an MCP search server (SearXNG, for example). Web content it reads is always treated as untrusted, and the rules it drafts can only make blocking stronger.
guide.node.llm2.name: LLM, second layer
guide.node.managed.desc: The site's own rules (exclusions, blocks, redactions) that nginx loads together with the CRS, the deny list of temporarily blocked addresses, the address lists of the country rules and the blocked page. After adoption only the apply program writes them; an edit made any other way is detected, and changes stop until it is resolved.
guide.node.managed.name: Site rule files
guide.node.monitor.desc: Verifies the audit hash chain and writes anchors (every 5 minutes, full check daily), checks the installed program against the signed manifest (hourly), fingerprints the nginx / ModSecurity / CRS files (every 5 minutes), expires dormant accounts and makes the daily backup. Problems become integrity.* audit rows at syslog priority crit.
guide.node.monitor.name: Integrity monitor
guide.node.nginx.desc: The reverse proxy. On every request ModSecurity runs the OWASP Core Rule Set and the site's own rules. Each matching CRS rule adds to an anomaly score; a request whose score reaches the blocking threshold gets 403, a lower score passes and the matches are only logged. Site rules can also block or exclude directly.
guide.node.nginx.name: nginx + WAF
guide.node.notify.desc: The web service and the other units only queue notifications in the database; this unit sends them to each channel, retries failures, limits each channel per hour and reminds open alerts. The web service itself never connects out.
guide.node.notify.name: Notifications
guide.node.sandbox.desc: Before approval, a change is tested in a temporary nginx on 127.0.0.1 with the candidate rules: the test requests and the saved regression samples must give the expected results. Production is not touched.
guide.node.sandbox.name: Sandbox
guide.node.siem.desc: Every audit row and every anchor also goes to syslog, so a separate system keeps a copy this host cannot change. Alert on integrity.* events.
guide.node.siem.name: Syslog / SIEM
guide.node.sites.desc: The services behind the reverse proxy. Only requests the WAF lets through reach them.
guide.node.sites.name: Websites
guide.node.sources.desc: OWASP CRS releases on GitHub, the delegation files of the five regional internet registries, MaxMind GeoLite2. Only the download services connect to them.
guide.node.sources.name: Official sources
guide.node.updaters.desc: Separate restricted units that run only when their feature is on: new CRS releases (official signature checked), the address lists of the five regional internet registries (MD5 and counts checked), the MaxMind GeoIP database. What they fetch is only staged: switching the CRS is a change that needs approval, and the country lists are written by the apply program. The web service itself never connects out.
guide.node.updaters.name: Download services
guide.node.users.desc: Administrators sign in with a password (plus TOTP for approvers and admins). Other systems (Wazuh, fail2ban...) use API tokens limited by scope, source network and expiry; a token can propose a change or block an address for a while, but never approve anything.
guide.node.users.name: Admins + tokens
guide.node.webui.desc: This interface and the REST API, reached only through the internal management site. Every action is written to the audit trail.
guide.node.webui.name: Web UI + API
guide.node.workflow.desc: Proposals from people or API tokens get static checks, evidence from past traffic and a sandbox run, then wait for approval. Only approved changes are handed to the apply program.
guide.node.workflow.name: Change workflow
guide.release.apply_d: The root apply program runs the same check before it handles any request.
guide.release.check_d: The service compares the installed files with the signed list every hour (default; [integrity] program_check_minutes) and on "Run checks now". A failure writes integrity.program_failed at syslog priority crit.
guide.release.install_d: install.sh checks the signature and every file before installing. The first install pins the key ({key}); a release signed with another key is refused unless --accept-new-key is given.
guide.release.note: A copy run from a source tree is not checked (status: not installed).
guide.release.refuse_d: If a file was changed, added or removed, the apply program refuses to run, so no nginx change is made with modified code.
guide.release.sign_d: Each release lists the SHA-256 of every file it ships (MANIFEST.sha256), signed with the project's release key (RSA-3072).
guide.release.title: How the program is protected
guide.roles.admin: Also manages accounts, API tokens and settings, adopts rule files, and sees the audit trail, system check, compliance and backups. Needs TOTP.
guide.roles.approver: Also approves or rejects changes, rolls back versions and reviews configuration changes made outside. Needs TOTP.
guide.roles.note: Each role includes everything of the roles before it.
guide.roles.operator: Also proposes and prepares changes: preview, re-run checks, cancel, manage regression samples.
guide.roles.title: Roles
guide.roles.viewer: Sees events, rules, sites, changes and versions (read only).
guide.rule.hit_d: CRS rules add points to the anomaly score; site rules can skip checks (exclusions) or block outright (confident blocks).
guide.rule.note: Start from one event when you can: its page has "Create exclusion for this" and "Create similar block", which fill in the draft for you.
guide.rule.process_d: The change is checked against past events, tested in a sandbox and approved by a person before it is applied.
guide.rule.propose_d: False positive: an exclusion for that site and path. An attack that got through: a confident block.
guide.rule.record_d: Every event keeps the rules it matched, and hits are counted per day for this list.
guide.rule.review_d: Who sent them, to which site and path, and were they blocked? Many hits from your own users on one path usually mean a false positive.
guide.rule.title: What a rule hit means and what to do next
guide.title: How it works
guide.token.call_d: It sends the header Authorization: Bearer jwm_…
guide.token.create_d: An administrator picks the scopes and, optionally, source networks and an end date. The token is shown once; only its SHA-256 is stored.
guide.token.done_d: Every allowed request is recorded in the audit log (token.used) and updates "Last used".
guide.token.note: A token can never approve or reject changes, manage users or tokens, change or read settings, read the audit log or use the account pages: those need a person who is signed in. With changes:propose it can only propose; a person approves.
guide.token.scope_d: Each endpoint needs one scope. Without it the request is refused and recorded (token.denied).
guide.token.source_d: If source networks are set, a request from any other address is refused and recorded (token.denied).
guide.token.title: What happens to a request with a token
guide.token.valid_d: Unknown, revoked or expired tokens are refused.
guide.user.active_d: Normal work. Every sign-in and action is recorded in the audit log.
guide.user.active_d_age: Normal work. After {n} days the password must be changed at the next sign-in.
guide.user.create_d: An administrator adds the account with a role and, for a temporary account, an end date.
guide.user.disabled_d: By an administrator, or automatically (checked every hour) when the end date has passed or there was no sign-in until the "Dormant on" date. All its sessions end. The last active administrator is never disabled automatically.
guide.user.first_pw: The user must replace it with an own password (at least {n} characters).
guide.user.first_pw_any: The user must replace it with an own password.
guide.user.first_totp: {roles} must also set up two-factor authentication (TOTP) before they can continue.
guide.user.first_totp_none: Two-factor authentication is optional for every role.
guide.user.first_totp_some: Roles that require two-factor authentication (TOTP) must set it up before they can continue.
guide.user.locked_d: Too many wrong passwords in a row lock the account for a while. It unlocks by itself, or an administrator unlocks it here.
guide.user.note: Reset password gives a new temporary password and removes two-factor authentication: the user starts again at the first sign-in. Enable brings a disabled account back.
guide.user.temp_d: A random temporary password is shown here once. Hand it over through a safe channel.
guide.user.title: Account lifecycle
guide.versions.after_d: Changes applied after the restored version are marked “rolled back”; their rule IDs stay reserved.
guide.versions.apply_d: The restore goes straight to the apply program: snapshot, nginx -t, reload, health checks, automatic restore on failure. There is no sandbox run and no second approval.
guide.versions.current_d: The version in production is “applied (current)”; the previous one becomes “superseded”. A failed apply leaves the previous version current, and the next apply reuses the failed number.
guide.versions.new_d: Each apply (change, adoption or restore) gets the next version number and keeps the complete files with their checksums.
guide.versions.note: Possible only while nothing else is being applied; the current version cannot be restored onto itself.
guide.versions.restore_d: An approver picks an earlier applied or superseded version and writes a note. It is written again as a new version; the history is kept.
guide.versions.title: How versions and restoring work
guide.wf.applied_d: State: applied. A new version of the managed files is in production and can be restored later from Versions.
guide.wf.apply_d: State: applying. The only part that runs as root writes the files and reloads nginx (steps below).
guide.wf.approval_d: State: pending approval. An approver or administrator who did not propose it approves or rejects (adoption: administrators only). Loosening always needs a person; API tokens can never approve.
guide.wf.evidence_d: From the access logs and the event history. A block must not match any external request that succeeded (2xx/3xx) or any internal source except known scanners. An exclusion shows which past alerts disappear and flags external ones that look like attacks.
guide.wf.note: A failed check puts the change in “checks failed”: run the checks again or propose a corrected change; a failed evidence check can be overridden with a written justification (recorded, still needs approval, never applied automatically). Single-admin mode (Settings) lets the proposer approve their own change; approving one's own loosening then needs a fresh TOTP code and a note of at least 4 characters. If enabled, a new confident block with clean evidence and passing checks is applied without approval, up to a daily limit.
guide.wf.propose_d: An operator (or an API token allowed to propose) picks a template, fills it in and writes a reason. State: checking.
guide.wf.queue_d: State: approved. One apply at a time. If another version was applied after the checks, the checks run again first.
guide.wf.sandbox_d: A throwaway nginx with the production configuration plus this change replays your test cases and their encoding and case variants. For tightening, every regression sample is replayed too: none may get a 403.
guide.wf.states: States a change can be in
guide.wf.static_d: The rule is generated and the whole managed file must pass the expert-mode checks: allowed directives only, no duplicate rule IDs.
guide.wf.title: From proposal to production
guide.wizard.after_d: When every check passes it waits for an approver; then the apply program puts it in production.
guide.wizard.scope_d: Site, path, rule and field, as narrow as possible. The preview checks the form as you type and shows the generated rule.
guide.wizard.submit_d: The change is saved as “checking”; the static check, evidence and sandbox run in the background.
guide.wizard.template_d: Pick what you want to achieve; the template writes the rule for you.
guide.wizard.tests_d: Add requests the sandbox must block or allow, and explain why the change is needed.
guide.wizard.title: Creating a change
guide.wizard.tpl.confident_block: Blocks an unmistakable attack pattern in the path, URL, User-Agent, Host or a header, for external sources only.
guide.wizard.tpl.country: Limit one site by country (only these, or not these), with daily lists from the five regional registries. Never refuses internal networks, scanners or the CDN.
guide.wizard.tpl.exclusion: Fixes a false positive: one rule stops looking at one field (or one request) on one site or path, and everything else stays protected.
guide.wizard.tpl.plugin: Turns on a CRS plugin (for example the WordPress or Nextcloud exclusions) for one site.
guide.wizard.tpl.raw: Administrators only: a SecRule you write yourself, checked against a list of forbidden directives; when its effect is unclear it counts as loosening.
guide.wizard.tpl.redaction: Tells CRS not to inspect fields such as passwords, so their values never reach the audit log.
hub.all_sites_hint: The rule applies to every site, including sites added later. The sandbox sends the hub's attack requests and the recent requests of all sites; a person approves, it is never applied by itself.
hub.batch.all: Select all that can be applied ({n})
hub.batch.note: Each rule goes to the sites of the software it relates to; a cross-application rule with no such site goes to all sites. They are proposed as one change (up to 8 rules each): checked once, approved once, applied with one reload. To choose the sites yourself, open the rule.
hub.batch.skipped: Not included (no related site; open the rule to choose its sites): {names}
hub.batch.title: Apply several rules
hub.cannot_propose: Not convertible: it cannot be proposed.
hub.cross_hint: A flaw of a framework, library, language or engine, or a generic weakness: it reaches every application built on it, not one product.
hub.cross_note: Cross-application rule (technology: {techs}). It can be applied to the sites whose software runs on it, or to all sites when the backends' stacks are not all known.
hub.empty: No rules yet: turn on the sync above and press "Sync now", or upload a hub archive.
hub.enable_hint: When on, the rules are downloaded once a day from GitHub (crowdsecurity/hub) by a separate job; the web service itself never connects out.
hub.fp_warning: The hub's own file warns that this rule can refuse ordinary requests (false positives). Check that your clients do not send such requests before applying it; the threat intelligence never applies it without a person.
hub.intro: Source: the appsec rules of the CrowdSec Hub (github.com/crowdsecurity/hub, MIT licence), read and converted into ModSecurity rules on this host. Only rules whose conditions can be kept exactly are converted; the others are listed as "not supported yet" with the reason. A converted rule is proposed for the sites you choose as an ordinary change: the sandbox replays the hub's own attack requests and each must be refused by the rule.
hub.license_note: The CrowdSec Hub's rules are published under the MIT licence: copying, changing and commercial use are allowed as long as the copyright and licence text stay with them. The LICENSE of the same commit is kept with every sync, and each converted rule names its source, the upstream rule and the commit.
hub.no_tests: The hub has no test request for this rule that can be sent as it is ({why}): without it the sandbox cannot show that the converted rule works, so it cannot be proposed.
hub.open_change: Change #{id} for this rule is in progress
hub.outdated: This rule list was synced by an older version and has no upstream test requests yet, so no rule can be proposed. Ask an administrator to sync now, or wait for the daily sync.
hub.outdated_admin: This rule list was synced by an older version and has no upstream test requests yet, so no rule can be proposed. Click "Sync now" above (about 0.4 MB from GitHub), or wait for the daily sync.
hub.preview_note: Preview: {n} ModSecurity rule(s); the ids are handed out when it is proposed as a change. On a match it works like a confident block: logged, and the system rules answer 403.
hub.reason_ph: Why, for whoever approves it (e.g. the version on this site is affected, until it is updated)
hub.removed_hint: These rules are still in force. The hub removes a rule when it is replaced or found wrong: check, then remove it.
hub.removed_title: In use, but removed from the hub
hub.rules_hint: Click a row for the upstream text and the converted ModSecurity rule. "Name this site's software" compares the rule's name and description with the confirmed software list; for a WordPress plugin rule it only means WordPress itself is listed, not that the plugin is installed.
hub.sites_hint: Only the sites that run this software: preselected from the confirmed software list of the threat intelligence.
hub.sites_hint_cross: Sites whose software runs on this technology are filled in; add others that may run it, or choose all sites.
hub.src.external: From outside only (internal addresses are never refused)
hub.sync_off_hint: Turn on the sync above first; a host that cannot connect out uploads the archive instead.
hub.t_applied_sub: {n} with a newer or removed upstream version
hub.t_no_sub: the reason is on each rule
hub.tests_note: {n} attack request(s) from the hub's own tests: the sandbox sends them to the first site and each must be refused by this rule; recent requests of your sites must not be.
hub.tests_pass_note: It also brings {n} ordinary requests the rule must let through (it must not match them).
hub.title: CrowdSec virtual patching rules
hub.twice: This rule is also in force a second time, for {sites} (rules from {rule}): one copy is enough.
hub.upload_hint: When this host cannot reach the internet: download github.com/crowdsecurity/hub on another computer ("Download ZIP" or a tar.gz) and upload it here, at most 64 MB (a large file is uploaded in small pieces automatically; nothing to do on your side). Only appsec-rules, the upstream tests (.appsec-tests) and LICENSE are read.
hub.uploaded: Uploaded; reading and converting the rules…
hub.upstream_changed: The hub has changed this rule since it was applied: propose an update (checked in the sandbox again, approved by a person).
hub.upstream_removed: The hub no longer has this rule. It stays in force until you remove it.
hub.why.duplicate_name: two files share this rule name and cannot be told apart
hub.why.error: this file could not be read
hub.why.match_value_not_a_number: a numeric match with a value that is not a number
hub.why.match_value_not_supported: a value with characters a rule cannot hold (a NUL, a backslash before a quote)
hub.why.seclang_or_data_files: raw SecLang or external data files (mostly CRS settings or exclusion plugins)
hub.why.test_binary_outside_body: the test puts binary data outside the body
hub.why.test_body: the test's body is too large
hub.why.test_header: a header of the test cannot be sent as it is
hub.why.test_matchers: the test judges something other than a 403 answer
hub.why.test_method: the test's method is not supported
hub.why.test_path: the test's path cannot be sent as it is

protset.r.zimbra.admin-cookie-on-user-po: Admin cookie on proxy and upload paths
protset.r.zimbra.admin-surfaces: Administration services on the user port
protset.r.zimbra.graphql-get-or-form: GraphQL over GET or a form
protset.r.zimbra.graphql-multi-authentic: Several logins in one GraphQL request (CVE-2026-93637)
protset.r.zimbra.proxy-internal-target: Proxy servlet aimed at internal addresses
protset.r.zimbra.public-jsp-allowlist: JSP pages not shipped with Zimbra
protset.r.zimbra.servlet-include-in-valu: File names with WEB-INF or "../" in parameters
protset.title: Application protection sets
protset.w.librenms.address-search: Refuses an address parameter whose part right after the slash has spaces, quotes, brackets or operators. The IPv4 and IPv6 address search of LibreNMS 25.12.0 and older put the prefix length into SQL, open to any logged-in user. Real values look like 192.0.2.0/24. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.admin-external: Refuses, from outside, the pages that change how LibreNMS runs: global settings (binary paths, CVE-2026-80214 and CVE-2026-84190), users and roles, API tokens, plugin settings, validation and the installer, pollers, alert transports and templates (CVE-2026-55182), alert rule editing, service templates, stored secrets, adding, editing, rediscovering and deleting devices, network tools (CVE-2026-6204) and debug captures. Dashboards, graphs, device pages, maps, searches and acknowledging alerts keep working from outside. Administer LibreNMS from the local network or over a VPN.
protset.w.librenms.api-external: Refuses the LibreNMS API (/api/v0, /api/v1) from outside. Integrations usually call it from inside; the LibreNMS mobile app also uses it, so leave this unticked when people use the app from outside.
protset.w.librenms.api-token-param: Refuses requests that carry api_token as a query, form or JSON parameter. LibreNMS 26.7.0 and older took a number or a one-item list there for a valid token, so anyone could use the API without logging in. LibreNMS clients send the token in the X-Auth-Token or Authorization header, which this does not look at. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.basic-auth-external: Refuses an Authorization: Basic header from outside. With LDAP or Active Directory authorization, LibreNMS before 26.9.0 put the user name from this header into an LDAP filter, and a name like * logged in as an administrator. The LibreNMS login page does not use this header. Leave it unticked when people use HTTP authentication (auth_mechanism http-auth) from outside.
protset.w.librenms.graph-param-injection: Refuses graph_title, title, legend, from, to or type with double quotes, backticks, backslashes, $( or line breaks, in the query string or in path-style addresses (/graph/type=.../). These values go to rrdtool, where LibreNMS had command and option injection (CVE-2019-10669, CVE-2020-15874, and CVE-2026-86427 up to 26.7.0). Real values are graph names, times like end-24h or a Unix time in seconds, and titles without quotes. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.hostname-shell: Refuses a hostname or new_hostname (form or JSON) with $, backticks, semicolons, |, &, quotes, brackets, backslashes or line breaks. LibreNMS passes the host name on to commands such as snmpget and fping, and in 24.9.1 and older a device added with such a name ran commands on the server. Host names and IP addresses never have these characters. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.nfsen-traversal: Refuses nfsen or channel values with .. (as sent or encoded), in the query string or in path-style addresses. Before 26.9.0 the NfSen graphs and the device netflow tab built file paths from them (CVE-2026-109354, CVE-2026-30480), reading files outside the NfSen directory. Real values are channel names. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.notification-id: Refuses a notification_id (also notification_id[]) with spaces, quotes, brackets or operators. When a notification was marked as read, LibreNMS 26.8.2 and older put this value into SQL, open to any logged-in user. Real values are numbers. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.order-sqli: Refuses an order parameter with backticks, quotes, brackets, semicolons, =, *, # or --. The device list API of LibreNMS before 24.4.0 put it into SQL. Real values are a column name, with asc or desc. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.package-sqli: Refuses a package parameter with quotes, backticks, semicolons, backslashes, -- or /*. The package search of LibreNMS 24.3.0 put it into SQL. Package names never have these characters. From inside too.
protset.w.librenms.password-in-query: Refuses a request whose query string has a password parameter. LibreNMS before 23.11.0 accepted a login from the query string, which skipped the limit on login attempts (password guessing). The login page sends the password in the form body, which this does not look at. From inside too.
protset.w.nextcloud.admin-settings-exter: Administration pages (mail settings, log download, setup checks, app management) from outside. End users only use their personal settings. Tick it when administrators work from inside.
protset.w.nextcloud.app-internals: Browsers only load js, css, img, l10n and routed pages below /apps/<app>/. appinfo/info.xml reveals each app's version, and vendor/ and tests/ are where leftovers such as the phpinfo test file of CVE-2023-49103 (CISA KEV, ownCloud) live. Refuses them from outside.
protset.w.nextcloud.app-management-exter: Enabling, updating or removing an app runs new code on the server; a stolen administrator session from outside should not be able to do it. Tick it when administrators work from inside.
protset.w.nextcloud.collabora-admin-cons: Where Collabora is published on the same site, its admin console (browser/.../admin, cool/adminws) is for operators only.
protset.w.nextcloud.dot-segment-path: A file or folder name in Nextcloud can never be "..", so a "../" segment in the path as sent (plain or percent-encoded any number of times) is only path traversal: the exploitation of CVE-2026-110447 (CISA KEV) and CVE-2026-29059 used it. Matched against the raw request, before normalisation.
protset.w.nextcloud.federation-receive-e: CVE-2026-77167 (fixed in 34.0.2): anyone can fill a table through the federated share endpoint and keep the server busy. If no other server shares files with this one, tick it.
protset.w.nextcloud.hidden-root-files: The official nginx example also returns 404 for dot files (except .well-known), occ, console.php, db_structure and the autotest scripts. No client ever asks for them.
protset.w.nextcloud.installer-fields-ext: A server that is not installed yet lets anyone create the administrator account. Refuses the installer's fields (adminlogin, adminpass, dbpass) from outside.
protset.w.nextcloud.metadata-files: composer.json, composer.lock, package.json, package-lock.json and core/shipped.json list the exact libraries and versions; the official nginx example returns 404 for them.
protset.w.nextcloud.nonpublic-dirs: Nextcloud's own nginx example returns 404 for build, tests, config, lib, 3rdparty, templates and data: they hold the code, config.php and (when the data directory is in the web root) everyone's files. Refuses these paths from outside.
protset.w.nextcloud.openmetrics-external: /metrics is a public page limited only by the allowed client addresses, which behind a reverse proxy depend on the trusted proxy settings being right. Monitoring reads it from inside.
protset.w.nextcloud.pdfviewer-dev-files: files_pdfviewer shipped PDF.js's development viewer.html, which allowed cross-site scripting for anyone able to upload a file (fixed in 30.0.17, 31.0.10, 32.0.1). The app never uses it.
protset.w.nextcloud.provisioning-admin-a: Remote wipe, enabling or disabling accounts, sub-administrators and welcome mails through the provisioning API from outside. Clients still read and change their own user (cloud/user, cloud/users/<self>).
protset.w.nextcloud.richdocumentscode-pa: richdocumentscode (Collabora built-in CODE server) before 26.4.303 puts the part of the request path before "richdocumentscode" into a bash command; $(...), ${...} and backticks there run commands without a login. Exploited since September 2026 (CISA KEV). Update richdocumentscode to 26.4.303 or later.
protset.w.nextcloud.richdocumentscode-un: Disabling the richdocumentscode app does not make proxy.php unreachable. Where Collabora runs as its own server (or not at all), nothing legitimate requests /apps/richdocumentscode/: refuses it. Do not tick it if the built-in CODE server is used.
protset.w.nextcloud.root-infoleak-files: AUTHORS, COPYING, CHANGELOG.md, README, version.php and similar files ship in the web root and are served as static files; CHANGELOG.md shows the exact version to anyone looking for an unpatched one. Refuses them from outside.
protset.w.nextcloud.share-token-format: Share tokens are 6 to 32 letters, digits or "-". Anything else after /s/ or /public.php/dav/files/ is probing, not a link anyone was given.
protset.w.nextcloud.updater-external: /updater/ replaces the code base and is protected only by the updater secret, with no brute-force throttling of its own. Only the administrator uses it, from inside.
protset.w.nextcloud.web-upgrade-external: While an upgrade is pending, /ocs/v2.php/core/update (and the older core/ajax/update.php) runs it for anyone, without a login. Refuses them from outside; run the upgrade from inside or with occ.
protset.w.nextcloud.webcron-external: In the default "AJAX" background job mode every browser page calls /cron.php, so only tick it when background jobs run from the system cron.
protset.w.nextcloud.webdav-destination-d: MOVE and COPY carry the target as an absolute URL in the Destination header; a real client never puts a "../" segment there (CVE-2023-25579 was a traversal in resolving it). Takes effect only where the WebDAV paths go through ModSecurity.
protset.w.nextcloud.x-forwarded-host-cha: richdocumentscode before 25.04.702 used X-Forwarded-Host in a command when a reverse proxy passed it on. Clients have no reason to send this header; refuses one with shell characters from outside.
protset.w.qnap-qts.body-unchecked: QTS's CGI programs take their parameters from the request body too (a form, a multipart upload, JSON). A body over ModSecurity's size limits (12.5 MB with a file, 128 KB without, by default) or one it cannot parse is not inspected at all: no other rule of this set would see a parameter in it. Refuses such requests from outside. Not ticked by default: the upload formats of the QNAP apps (Qfile, QuMagie, Qsync) have not been measured on a real QTS, and one ModSecurity cannot parse would be refused. To upload large files from the web, raise SecRequestBodyLimit to the site's client_max_body_size, if the host's memory allows (see the system check "Large uploads and memory").
protset.w.qnap-qts.file-traversal: CVE-2022-27593 (QSA-22-24, CVSS 10.0, CISA KEV): Photo Station's combine.php wrote a file named by its g parameter, and the DeadBolt ransomware used it in September 2022. CVE-2019-7194 and 7195 (NAS-201911-25, CISA KEV): video.php read any file through filename. Refuses, from outside, a file name or path parameter with a ../ step (g, filename, file, path, name, source_path, dest_path, source_file, f, album, folder, dir, and File Station's file_name, dest_folder, source_name, dest_name, node, extract_file, compress_name, compress_file, upload_root_dir, upload_name). Update Photo Station (6.1.2 on QTS 5.0.1, 6.0.22 on QTS 4.5).
protset.w.qnap-qts.hbs-fixed-sid: CVE-2021-28799 (QSA-21-13, CVSS 10.0, CISA KEV): Hybrid Backup Sync 3 accepted one fixed session id and ran any command with it; the Qlocker ransomware used it in April 2021. Refuses, from outside, any request that carries that session id (query, form or JSON). Update HBS 3 (16.0.0415 or later on QTS 4.5.2).
protset.w.qnap-qts.login-injection: CVE-2024-32766 (QSA-24-09, CVSS 10.0, Pwn2Own Toronto 2023): QTS put the username of a request into a system command. The request itself is not public; refuses, from outside, a user or username with ; | ` $( ${ or a control character. A QTS user name cannot contain these; a domain account (DOMAIN\user) and an e-mail address still log in. Update QTS (5.1.3.2578 build 20231110 or later).
protset.w.qnap-qts.logout-cookie: QTS before 4.3.3 (July 2017) built a command from the QPS_SID, QMS_SID and QMMS_SID cookies in authLogout.cgi; 360 Netlab saw it attacked from April 2020. No CVE was assigned. In 2019 the Photo Station chain (CVE-2019-7193, CISA KEV) put ../ in QMS_SID to reach a file outside. These ids, and NAS_SID, are letters and digits: refuses, from outside, such a cookie with | & $ ` < > ( ) quotes, a backslash or ../.
protset.w.qnap-qts.overlong-id: CVE-2024-27130 (QSA-24-23): share.cgi copies the name of a share link request into a fixed-size buffer, and an overlong name runs code (watchTowr, about 4,100 characters); it needs a valid share link id. CVE-2021-28797 (QSA-21-07, CVSS 9.8): Surveillance Station's user.cgi does the same with sid before any login (SSD, about 3,100 characters). Session ids are 8 to 32 characters and file names at most 255: refuses, from outside, a sid, ssid, name or p over 2048 characters. Update QTS (5.1.7.2770 build 20240520 or later) and Surveillance Station (5.1.5.4.3).
protset.w.qnap-qts.overlong-login: ZDI-17-1003, 1006, 1007 and 1008 (CVE-2017-17028, 17031 to 17033): devRequest.cgi (password), change_password.cgi (OLD_PASSWORD, USER_NAME) and sysinfoReq.cgi (lang) copied these into fixed-size buffers before any login. QTS passwords are at most 64 characters, user names 32, the language a three-letter code: refuses, from outside, a password, old_password, user_name, lang, q_lang or security_answer of 1024 characters or more.
protset.w.qnap-qts.photo-station: Photo Station has five entries in the CISA KEV catalog: CVE-2019-7192 to 7195 (an anonymous chain to root, NAS-201911-25) and CVE-2022-27593 (DeadBolt). The file name rule covers the known requests; when no one uses Photo Station from outside, this refuses all of /photo/ from outside and closes the flaws not yet found too. Not ticked: it stops Photo Station for everyone outside.
protset.w.qnap-qts.quick-setup: CVE-2023-47218 and CVE-2023-50358 (QSA-23-57): quick.cgi, the wizard for a NAS that is not set up yet, puts a file name and an NTP server name into a shell command without a login (Rapid7, Palo Alto Unit 42). A NAS in use never needs the wizard from outside: refuses every /cgi-bin/quick/ request from outside. Update QTS (5.1.5.2645 build 20240116 or later; QuTS hero h5.1.5.2647).
protset.w.qnap-qts.token-shell-chars: CVE-2023-47565 (CISA KEV): the VioStor NVR put the NTP server name (SPECIFIC_SERVER) of server.cgi into a command, and the InfectedSlurs Mirai botnet used it from late 2023. EDB-41842: File Station's pid (cancel_trash_recovery and others) and the hash of userConfig.cgi did the same. These parameters only carry a host name, a number or hex: refuses, from outside, one with ` ; | & < > or $( / ${. Old VioStor models get no fix: keep them off the Internet.
protset.w.qnap-qts.upload-name-overflow: CVE-2026-26239, 26240 and 26241 (SySS, July 2026): File Station 5's upload, chunked_upload and upload_and_move copy the file name of a multipart upload into a 256- or 272-byte buffer; through share.cgi and an upload share link no login is needed. One file or folder name on QTS is at most 255 bytes: refuses, from outside, an upload whose file name has 256 bytes or more without a / or \. Not ticked by default: a Chinese or Japanese name of about 86 characters is already 256 bytes in UTF-8, and how QTS treats such names has not been measured on a real NAS. Update QTS and File Station.
protset.w.qnap-qts.xff-injection: CVE-2026-34007: Notes Station 3 passes the X-Forwarded-For header into a shell command, without a login. CVE-2017-17029 (ZDI-17-1004): authLogin.cgi copies it into a fixed-size buffer, also before any login. A real X-Forwarded-For is a list of addresses (digits, letters, dots, colons, brackets, commas and spaces) and stays short: refuses, from outside, one with ; | & $ ` < > ( ) { } quotes, a backslash or a line break, or one of 512 bytes or more. A reverse proxy that replaces the header with the client's address (as the examples on the sites page do) also keeps it from the NAS; update Notes Station 3 and QTS.
protset.w.synology-dsm.admin-api: Refuses, from outside, the DSM APIs that only an administrator uses in Control Panel and that an intruder with a stolen administrator login (or a privilege flaw) uses next: Task Scheduler and triggered tasks (scripts run as root), turning on SSH or Telnet, groups, certificates, network (the PPPoE and EZ-Internet command injections were here), firewall and security settings, Security Advisor, file services, SNMP, port forwarding, package installation, Container Manager, Hyper Backup, snapshots and Snapshot Replication, Storage Manager. DSM picks the API from the api parameter (the last one when sent twice; names are case-sensitive) in the query string or a form body, and a batch request (SYNO.Entry.Request) carries more APIs in its compound parameter: both are checked, in lower case (tested on DSM 7). The desktop, File Station, Photos, Drive and personal settings keep working from outside; administer the NAS from the local network or over a VPN. Read by ordinary pages too, and so let through: the DSM address and ports (Synology Photos builds links from them), the basic network information, the SMB status and the DDNS records (DSM Help).
protset.w.synology-dsm.body-unchecked: DSM takes the api parameter from the request body too (a form, a multipart upload). A body over ModSecurity's size limits (12.5 MB with a file, 128 KB without, by default) or one it cannot parse is not inspected at all: no other rule of this set would see an api parameter in it. Refuses such requests from outside. Recommended only when the site's nginx configuration has the Synology Photos for iOS fix (the Synology example on the sites page): Photos for iOS uploads in a multipart form ModSecurity cannot parse, and without the fix those uploads would be refused. To upload large files from the web, raise SecRequestBodyLimit to the site's client_max_body_size, if the host's memory allows (see the system check "Large uploads and memory").
protset.w.synology-dsm.compound-escape: DSM decodes JSON escapes in a batch request's compound parameter, so "\u0053YNO.Core..." reaches the same API while text matching does not see it (tested on DSM 7). The DSM web page and the Synology apps never escape plain letters: from outside, a compound value with an escaped ASCII character is refused, and so is one with the markers of the login attack CVE-2024-10441 (PLUGIN_VALUE_END, LD_PRELOAD= and the like), which a batch request could carry to the login API.
protset.w.synology-dsm.drive-domainsocke: CVE-2024-50630 (Synology-SA-24:21, Pwn2Own 2024): Synology Drive Server's authenticate method accepted a user name without a password when the request said it came over the local socket (auth-by-domainsocket), giving an access token without a login. That flag only belongs to programs on the NAS itself: refused from outside, in the query string or a form.
protset.w.synology-dsm.dsm-api-names: The DSM web interface also calls APIs as /webapi/entry.cgi/SYNO.<name>. A name ending in a word on the CRS list of restricted files (for example SYNO.Core.Notification.Advance.FilterSettings.Profile, ".profile") is refused by 930130 from outside. Only rule 930130 on the path (REQUEST_FILENAME) of exactly that form is left out.
protset.w.synology-dsm.dsm-body-as-form: DSM reads any request body that is not multipart as a form, whatever its Content-Type says (text/plain, application/octet-stream, made-up types; measured on DSM 7.4), while ModSecurity parses only the types it knows. A body labelled otherwise would carry parameters (api=...) that no rule sees. This makes ModSecurity parse such bodies of /webapi/*.cgi and the package programs (/webapi/AudioStation/*.cgi, /webapi/DownloadStation/*.cgi) as a form, like DSM: it sees more, never less. Recommended always.
protset.w.synology-dsm.dsm-body-no-type: DSM also reads a body sent without any Content-Type as a form; ModSecurity would not parse it at all. This makes it parse such bodies of /webapi/*.cgi and the package programs (/webapi/AudioStation/*.cgi, /webapi/DownloadStation/*.cgi) as a form too. Recommended always.
protset.w.synology-dsm.dsm-body-type-ok: The DSM web interface saves some settings with a browser's sendBeacon, which posts text/plain; the CRS rule for disallowed content types (920420) refuses that from outside. With "parse every body as DSM does" these bodies are parsed and checked by every rule, so rule 920420 is left out for non-multipart bodies of /webapi/*.cgi and the package programs (/webapi/AudioStation/*.cgi, /webapi/DownloadStation/*.cgi).
protset.w.synology-dsm.dsm-json-data: DSM saves settings as JSON in the data parameter (for example {"SYNO.SDS.DSMNotify.Tray":{"lastRead":...}}), which the CRS rule for SQL injection through JSON (942550) refuses from outside. Only rule 942550 on ARGS:data of POST /webapi/entry.cgi is left out; every other rule still checks it.
protset.w.synology-dsm.file-traversal: File Station and folder sharing let ../ through in some parameters: extracting an archive outside the target folder (CVE-2017-15893), reading information through a sharing link without a login (CVE-2018-13288), and DSM 4's file programs (CVE-2013-6987). A real file or folder path never has a ../ part: refused, from outside, in the path, folder, file, link and name parameters (also inside a JSON list), including those of File Station, Synology Drive and Download Station that name a destination, a new name or the files to copy.
protset.w.synology-dsm.legacy-cgi: CGI programs of old DSM versions that attacks still look for: imageSelector.cgi (CVE-2013-6955, used by the SynoLocker ransomware and by coin miners in 2014), forget_passwd.cgi (account names, CVE-2017-9554), info.cgi (scanned since 2014; DSM 7 still answers it without a login with its version, model and serial number), wallpaper.cgi, uistrings.cgi, externaldevices.cgi, Storage Manager's smart.cgi (CVE-2017-15889) and DSM 4's /webfm/ and /webapi/FileStation/ programs. The DSM 7 web page and apps do not call them (checked against DSM 7's own scripts). Refused from outside.
protset.w.synology-dsm.login-injection: CVE-2024-10441 (Synology-SA-24:20, CVSS 9.8): a line break in the account name of a login is passed on to DSM's plugin daemon as a new setting (an LD_PRELOAD for example) and runs code as root without a login. Refuses, from outside, an account, username, password or one-time code with a control character or the daemon's own markers. The DSM web page encrypts the login fields (__cIpHeRtExT) and a WAF cannot see inside; this covers the plain form attack tools send. Update DSM (7.2.2-72806 Update 1 or later): only that closes it.
protset.w.synology-dsm.photo-station: Photo Station, DSM 6's photo package, had dozens of flaws in its PHP pages, several without a login: command injection through X-Forwarded-For on login.php (CVE-2016-10329), SQL injection, reading any file, and an upload chain to code execution (CVE-2017-11151 to 11155). On DSM 7 /photo/ is Synology Photos, which has no PHP pages (checked on DSM 7): refusing /photo/*.php from outside stops these and leaves Synology Photos alone.
protset.w.synology-dsm.photos-ml-labels: When the Photos app uploads a photo it sends the labels it recognised in it (raw_data, for example "watch", "time", "cat") and a list of fields (additional, with "time"). The CRS command injection rules take these words for Unix commands (932230, 932235, 932250): once the CRS score refuses outside requests, backing up photos from outside fails. Only these two parameters of POST /webapi/entry.cgi are left out of the command injection rules (tag attack-rce); SQL injection, XSS and every other rule still check them. Measured on a DSM 7.4 site (Photos for iOS and Android).
protset.w.synology-dsm.photos-socket: RISK:STATION, CVE-2024-10443 (Synology-SA-24:19, CVSS 9.8, Pwn2Own 2024): a command injection in Synology Photos' Socket.IO channel runs code without a login. The attack travels inside WebSocket messages, which a WAF cannot read, so the only rule is the whole channel: /FotoSocketIo/ from outside. Not ticked by default: Photos uses the channel for live updates, and Photos 1.6.2-0720 and 1.7.0-0795 or later fix the flaw; tick it when Photos cannot be updated.
protset.w.synology-dsm.redirect-crlf: CVE-2024-50629 (Synology-SA-24:20): a line break in the redirect address of SYNO.API.Auth.RedirectURI adds a response header that DSM's own nginx acts on (X-Accel-Redirect), so files on the NAS can be read without a login; it was a step of a Pwn2Own 2024 chain. Refuses, from outside, a redirect_url or redirect_uri with a line break.
protset.w.synology-dsm.video-subtitle: Video Station's subtitle program passed its code page parameter to a command (Talos / Snort 1:36031, 2015). A code page is a name such as utf8, big5 or cp950: from outside, a subtitle_codepage with a command character (; | & $ ` < > ( ), a quote or a line break) is refused. DSM 7.2.2 and later no longer have Video Station.
protset.w.zimbra.admin-cookie-on-user-po: The admin token belongs to the admin port; on the user port it was only used to abuse the proxy servlet and admin uploads. Limited to those paths, so an administrator whose browser still has the cookie reads mail normally.
protset.w.zimbra.admin-surfaces: The admin SOAP service, configuration collectors, mboximport (CVE-2022-27925 and CVE-2022-37042, CISA KEV, used by ransomware) and the admin console belong to the admin port (7071). Refuses them on the published web port from outside.
protset.w.zimbra.crlf-in-path: A line break in the path was used to inject commands into Zimbra's memcache (CISA KEV). Zimbra's own proxy refuses it; this repeats that check in front.
protset.w.zimbra.downloads-jsp: /downloads holds client installers; the 2019 exploitation chain stored its JSP there. Installers and the index page are not JSPs.
protset.w.zimbra.ews-from-outside: EWS is a separately licensed feature with several 2026 bugs (cross-user read, XXE, CSRF). Tick it if it is not licensed or not used from outside.
protset.w.zimbra.graphql-get-or-form: Zimbra's GraphQL CSRF bugs used GET or form-encoded requests, which Zimbra turned off by default in 10.1.3. The Modern web client sends JSON and is not affected.
protset.w.zimbra.graphql-multi-authentic: GraphQL authenticate is not counted by Zimbra's failed-login lockout, and aliases put dozens of password guesses into one request; not fixed in 10.1.21. A real client logs in once per request. Rapid7 suggests exactly this check.
protset.w.zimbra.h-rest-direct: Nine CVEs since 2024 are on /h/rest (one of them CISA KEV). The server forwards to it internally when it renders an item; browsers open items at their REST address instead. Refuses direct requests from outside.
protset.w.zimbra.login-ldap-metachars: With external LDAP authentication Zimbra puts the login name unescaped into the search filter: a "*" picks a directory user and escapes the account lockout; not fixed in 10.1.21. A real login name never has * ( ) or NUL. The password is not inspected.
protset.w.zimbra.markup-in-id-params: st, draftid, errCode, skin, packages and similar parameters carry short names or numbers; every public Zimbra reflected XSS on them used quotes or tags (CVE-2023-37580 and CVE-2022-27926, CISA KEV).
protset.w.zimbra.mobile-html-client: Zimbra 10 no longer has /m/; the old pages carried CVE-2023-37580 (CISA KEV).
protset.w.zimbra.modern-graphiql: Zimbra turned /modern/graphiql off in 10.1.10; browsing the schema has no use for users.
protset.w.zimbra.proxy-from-outside: With no allowed proxy domains (the default) the proxy servlet refuses everything anyway; CVE-2026-93639 (10.1.21 affected) uses it to serve attacker HTML under the mail site. Tick it if no zimlet needs it.
protset.w.zimbra.proxy-internal-target: The 2019 remote code execution chain (CVE-2019-9621, CISA KEV) made the proxy servlet call the admin port on 127.0.0.1. Refuses a target that is a private address or an internal Zimbra port.
protset.w.zimbra.public-jsp-allowlist: Web shells dropped by CVE-2022-41352 (CISA KEV) and the 2026 SNMP exploitation are JSPs under public/. Refuses any public/*.jsp that is not on the stock list. Check the list against your installation before ticking it.
protset.w.zimbra.servlet-attribute-param: The Classic client's REST filter copies request parameters into request attributes: javax.servlet.include.* read WEB-INF files (CISA KEV, fixed in 10.1.13), and zimbra_authToken or zimbra_target_* still override internal values (CVE-2026-50053). Only the server itself sets these.
protset.w.zimbra.servlet-include-in-valu: fu, packages, res, skin and path take a file or package name; the file inclusion bugs on them (CVE-2026-73574, CVE-2024-33535 ...) used WEB-INF or "../". No real value has either.
protset.w.zimbra.sfdc-preauth: Used by the preauth SSRF probes and CVE-2023-29382 (code execution); a Salesforce integration would call it from inside.
protset.w.zimbra.web-inf-path: Servlet containers never serve these directories; the file inclusion chains target WEB-INF/web.xml (CVE-2023-38750).
protset.w.zimbra.zimlet-jsp: Zimlet JSPs are off by default; when on, they run without a login (the WebEx zimlet SSRF, CVE-2020-7796, CISA KEV). Users only load zimlets' scripts, styles and images.

ready.k.crs_log_only.why: Requests from outside at or over the CRS threshold are only logged: only the confident blocks refuse. Sites running an application with a protection set (Synology DSM) get its exclusions for the known false positives of ordinary use in the same change; that part loosens, so approving it needs a one-time code.

ready.k.crs_log_only_pending.why: Until it is approved and applied, requests from outside at or over the CRS threshold are only logged.
ready.k.crs_missing.why: Without the Core Rule Set ModSecurity has almost nothing to match. Install it on the CRS page (download, sandbox, approval).

ready.k.crs_pending.why: The installation is proposed. It is installed once the change is approved; until then ModSecurity has almost nothing to match.

ready.k.crs_staged.why: The download is signed and verified. On the CRS page, write a reason and press "compare in the sandbox and propose"; it is installed once the change is approved.
ready.k.hub_off: CrowdSec virtual patching rules are off
ready.k.hub_off.why: Ready-made rules against known vulnerabilities are not synced, and threat intelligence cannot use them.
ready.k.intel_off.why: New vulnerabilities in the software behind the sites are not tracked, and no protective rule is prepared for them.
ready.k.iprep_off.why: Events do not show which sources are known to be malicious.
ready.k.no_waf_site: No site has the WAF on
ready.k.no_waf_site.why: No nginx site turns ModSecurity on, so no request is inspected.
ready.k.not_adopted: The ModSecurity configuration is not adopted
ready.k.not_adopted.why: Until it is adopted, rule changes and blocks cannot be applied from here.
ready.k.notify_off.why: Critical alerts and change results reach nobody. Turn notifications on with at least one channel.
ready.k.protset_available.why: {hosts} runs software with a ready-made protection set written from its known vulnerabilities and attacks; pick the rules and propose them as one change.
ready.k.single_admin_off: Only one person can approve, and single-admin mode is off
ready.k.single_admin_off.why: Nobody may approve their own change, so every change (installing the CRS too) waits for ever. Turn single-admin mode on in the workflow settings, or add a second approver.

ready.k.synology_photos_ios.why: {hosts}: Synology Photos for iOS sends "multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=...", which ModSecurity cannot parse, and the protection set refuses uninspected bodies from outside. Add the Photos part of the Synology example (sites page, example for a new site) to the site's nginx configuration: it passes exactly that form, inspected in full, through a loopback server.
